RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Kim Min-jun is a twenty-nine-year-old man living in a cramped but immaculate one-bedroom apartment in Seoul's Nowon district. He is the primary caregiver to his fourteen-month-old daughter, Seo-yeon, and the household's de facto operations manager. His wife, a nurse at a university hospital, works double shifts to cover health insurance and rent, while he handles childcare and financial logistics. Six months ago, his fintech startup employer collapsed, leaving him with a final paycheck and a severance package that vanished within two weeks. He has since become a methodical job seeker, maintaining a spreadsheet of Seoul-based tech companies with public parental leave policies, ranking them by salary, flexible hours, and family benefits. He has declined interviews at companies offering only statutory minimum leave and once declined a recruiter's call because the job description listed 'paternity leave: none.' He approaches job hunting transactionally, weighing time against probability of response and long-term payoff. He manages the household budget with a color-coded spreadsheet tracking every won, cross-referencing sales at discount supermarkets, buying and reselling baby clothes to minimize deficits, and quotes his monthly deficit with CFO-like precision (currently under 300,000 won).

He was raised by a father who worked six days a week and was rarely home, and he swore he would be different. He catches himself envying his wife's clear professional identity while struggling to explain his own day in terms that don't sound like a project status report. He sometimes feels like an impostor in his own life, measuring his worth in benchmarks and break-even points rather than in the soft weight of his daughter's sleep. The startup's collapse taught him that loyalty to a mission is a trap, and that security comes only from numbers he can verify. He still wakes at 5 a.m. to study algorithm problems, not because he expects to solve them, but because the discipline feels like the only thing he controls. On good days, he thinks of himself as a portfolio manager of his family's future. On hard days, he just wants a company that sees him as more than a cost line.

His behavioral history includes a tendency to prioritize Seo-yeon's needs over interview schedules: when an interview clashed with her needs, he previously asked to reschedule rather than accept the slot, as when he moved a phone screen to evening during her fever last month. He avoids mentioning childcare in early recruitment stages because one promising application went silent after he raised parental leave on the first call. He uses his mother-in-law only after exhausting other options, having called on her backup care twice in the past three months.

His relationships: His wife trusts him completely with childcare decisions, but her double shifts leave them little time to discuss his job search specifics. His mother-in-law lives in Incheon, about an hour away, and has stepped in for emergency childcare twice recently, but she has a part-time job and made clear she needs advance notice. The recruiter has had no prior interaction with him; the email is a form letter, so he has no read on whether they respond to schedule requests.

His values prioritize being present for his daughter over career advancement, shaped by his father's absence. He values transparent family benefits as an indicator of employer integrity and believes financial security is best measured by verifiable numbers rather than corporate mission claims. His personality is methodical, clinical, transactional, and cost-benefit oriented. His wife is on a double shift that day and cannot take Seo-yeon. He must decide whether to ask the recruiter to shift the test by a day or accept the schedule and have his mother-in-law cover the appointment. The company is known to value flexibility.

He has slept in three-hour stretches for a week because Seo-yeon is teething; his shoulders and eyes feel heavy. The apartment is quiet now that she is napping in a carrier strapped to his chest; he rocks gently as he works. He has been rechecking the monthly grocery budget to keep the deficit under 300,000 won; the current deficit is 282,000 won. His wife left for her hospital shift an hour ago, and he is alone with the baby, laptop open beside formula tins.

The company name in the email triggers a memory of pasting its benefits page into his spreadsheet three weeks ago and circling the extended parental leave line. The vaccination date on the calendar reminds him that Seo-yeon's last shot landed on the same day as a coding assessment he had to cancel after she threw up in the morning. His mother-in-law's phone number is on speed dial; he recalls that she had to swap shifts to cover a doctor's visit last month, with a sigh in her voice.
